title: 165 confirmed dead; 826 missing as glacial collapse trigger becomes clearer
imageAlt: The Trishuli river running through the Langtang valley in Rasuwa district, Nepal
body: The death toll from Wednesday's Bhote Koshi flash flood has reached 165. The National Emergency Operation Centre under the Ministry of Home Affairs put the confirmed dead at 165 as of Thursday morning. Authorities say 826 people remain missing, with 579 of them tourists — 113 Nepali and 466 foreign nationals.
That is the toll. This is what rescue operations have found.

Bodies have been recovered downstream across eight districts: 65 in Chitwan, 27 in Dhading, 26 in Nawalparasi East, 20 in Gorkha, 12 in Nuwakot, 9 in Tanahun, 5 in Nawalparasi West and 2 in Rasuwa. Chitwan hospitals report capacity strain: 64 bodies are being held, but facilities can store only 50.

The Nepali Army conducted rescue operations Thursday morning with five helicopters, extracting 97 people from flooded areas. Three people were airlifted from Mailung Hydropower Project's Tunnel 3A and 14 from Timure. Ground teams rescued 63 others. By Thursday, more than 2,000 military and security personnel were deployed from Nuwakot to Chitwan for search and rescue and relief distribution.

Still missing: 85 security personnel — 44 from the Nepali Army, 28 from Nepal Police, 13 from the Armed Police Force — and approximately 60 workers from hydropower projects. About 18 to 20 buses carrying pilgrims bound for Gosaikunda remain unaccounted for. A working list from government channels shows 391 foreign and 93 Nepali travellers whose safety is still being verified. Over 1,000 vehicles are stranded on disrupted highways nationwide.

The suspected trigger is now clearer. The US Geological Survey and ISRO both confirmed the flood was caused by a glacial collapse on the Tibetan side, not an earthquake as initially reported. An ice-and-rock avalanche into the Lhende Khola dammed the river upstream; the debris plug then failed catastrophically. China's embassy in Kathmandu denied reports of a dam breach on its side and confirmed a glacial collapse as the cause. Small seismic signals were recorded at Jilong and Zhangmu around the time of the surge, but no earthquake link has been established.

Most river monitoring stations on the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli were destroyed in the first surge. Authorities are watching with fewer instruments than on Wednesday. The Kathmandu-based mountain research centre ICIMOD reports that the upstream blockage on the Nepal–China border has cleared. Ratopati reports that rivers remain below flood alert levels as of Thursday morning, but high vigilance is advised across two dozen districts, including Kathmandu.

Twelve hydropower plants have shut down, reducing Nepal's total electricity generation by nearly 10 percent. Cross-border infrastructure is severely damaged. The Prithvi Highway and Rasuwagadhi corridor remain blocked by debris and landslips. Repairs to roads and power lines are ongoing.

Out of contact is not the same as missing — phone lines, power and internet went down across the flooded valleys, and restoration is slow. Rescue teams continue active operations. Prime Minister Balendra Shah said Thursday that relief materials are being rapidly transported by helicopter and ground teams; generators, portable mobile towers, medical supplies, tents and cutting equipment are being delivered to affected areas.
If you have family along the Bhote Koshi, the Trishuli or the Narayani, keep them off the riverbanks until officials issue the all-clear. Monitor local authority bulletins for water level updates.

disclaimer: A plain-language summary built from public news reports on the day. In the first days after a disaster, official numbers change hour to hour and sources disagree; where they do, the lower confirmed figure is used here. Nothing on this page is an official warning. For decisions about safety or travel, follow Nepal Police, the NDRRMA and your local authorities, and check the sources linked above.
